lead: A chopper is a switch between a DC source and load, opening and closing thousands of times a second. Closed, the load sees the source voltage; open, almost zero. The average load voltage equals source voltage times the fraction of each period the switch is closed. This idea runs DC motor drives, chargers, LED drivers and solar trackers. Names: DC chopper, buck chopper, DC-DC converter.
prereq: You need the power MOSFET and IGBT as switches, with their gate drive (see Power BJT, MOSFET and IGBT), and the idea of an average voltage from a switched source (see Diode rectifiers: half-wave, full-wave and bridge).

sections.h3: The chopper and its duty ratio

blocks.text: A basic chopper has a DC source V<sub>s</sub>, a controlled switch (MOSFET or IGBT with gate driver), a freewheeling diode D<sub>f</sub>, and the load. The switch is fully on (almost zero voltage) or fully off (zero current), so it wastes little power as heat.

Switch on: load tied to source, v<sub>o</sub>(t) = V<sub>s</sub>. Switch off: inductive load current cannot stop instantly, so it turns through D<sub>f</sub> and load voltage falls to about −V<sub>d</sub>, close to zero. D<sub>f</sub> is also called flywheel or catch diode.
The current formula assumes an R-L load with an inductor large enough to keep current continuous, or a chopper feeding an L-C filter.
T = Ton + Toff = 1/fs , D = Ton / T , Vo = D·Vs , Io = Vo / R = D·Vs / R

T is switching period in seconds; f<sub>s</sub> is switching frequency in hertz; T<sub>on</sub> and T<sub>off</sub> are on and off times in seconds; D is duty ratio, 0 to 1; V<sub>s</sub> is source voltage in volts; V<sub>o</sub> is average load voltage in volts; R is load resistance in ohms; I<sub>o</sub> is average load current in amperes, for continuous inductor current.

V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub> is an average. The load voltage is a pulse train between V<sub>s</sub> and about 0; a moving-coil DC voltmeter shows only the mean. At D = 0 load gets nothing; at D = 1 full source. With an inductor keeping current continuous, P<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>·I<sub>o</sub> = D²·V<sub>s</sub>²/R watts. For a purely resistive load the current pulses with voltage, so average power is D·V<sub>s</sub>²/R, not V<sub>o</sub>·I<sub>o</sub>.

Open loop, output obeys D·V<sub>s</sub> and nothing corrects it; input sag or load change shifts V<sub>o</sub>. Closed loop measures V<sub>o</sub>, compares with reference V<sub>ref</sub>, amplifies error, and lets error set D. Three strategies set D.

items: Constant-frequency pulse-width (time-ratio) control. An oscillator fixes T and only Ton moves. A comparator compares the error signal with a sawtooth of period T; where they cross, the switch turns off, so a larger error gives a wider pulse. Ripple frequency is fixed, filter design is easy, switching loss is predictable. Most controller ICs do this.

Variable-frequency control. Ton is fixed and fs changes. Pulse energy per cycle is constant and switch conduction time is known, but the filter must suit the lowest frequency used, and noise spreads across a band that is harder to filter and clear for EMI.

Current-limit control. The switch turns off when inductor or load current reaches upper limit Imax and back on at lower limit Imin. Output follows the current band; a short circuit is limited cycle by cycle, so chargers and motor drives use it. Frequency varies with load and source voltage; ripple current is fixed by the chosen band Imax − Imin.

blocks.text: Choppers are named by what they do to voltage.

items: Step-down (buck) chopper: Vo < Vs. The switch-diode pair sits before an L-C filter and the inductor averages the pulse down; see Buck converter.
Step-up (boost) chopper: Vo > Vs. The inductor charges from source with switch on, then sits in series with source through a diode; see Boost converter.
Step-down/step-up (buck-boost) chopper: output above or below input, reversed polarity; see Buck-boost and Cuk converters.
Cuk chopper: same gain, a capacitor in the middle, smooth current at both ports; also in Buck-boost and Cuk converters.

blocks.text: Two conduction modes describe inductor current. In continuous conduction mode (CCM) that current never reaches zero inside a period. In discontinuous conduction mode (DCM) current falls to zero before period ends and rests until next pulse, so gain depends on load and D.

In DC motor drives, choppers are also classed by the quadrants of the load’s v-i plane they work in, because a motor must send its braking energy back to the source. Class A works in the first quadrant only (v and i positive): the plain step-down chopper. Class B works in the second (v positive, i reversed) and returns braking energy to the source. Class C (quadrants 1 and 2) and class D (quadrants 1 and 4) each use two switches and two diodes, and class E, a full bridge of four switches, works in all four. The gains of the converter families are derived in the next chapters.

Right: two pulse trains of 200 volt pulses 0.4 milliseconds wide, one with a 1 millisecond period and average 80 volts, one with a 0.5 millisecond period and average 160 volts.

examples.question: A chopper feeds an R-L load (R = 10 Ω, inductor large enough for continuous current) from 200 V DC. f<sub>s</sub> = 1 kHz, T<sub>on</sub> = 0.4 ms. (a) Find D, V<sub>o</sub>, I<sub>o</sub> and P<sub>o</sub>. (b) At 2 kHz with same T<sub>on</sub>, find D, V<sub>o</sub> and P<sub>o</sub>.
steps: Continuous current: I<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>/R = 80 V / 10 Ω = 8 A.
Both V<sub>o</sub> and I<sub>o</sub> doubled, so power rose four times.
examples.answer: At 1 kHz: D = 0.4, V<sub>o</sub> = 80 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 8 A, P<sub>o</sub> = 640 W. At 2 kHz: D = 0.8, V<sub>o</sub> = 160 V, P<sub>o</sub> = 2560 W. This assumes continuous current; for a pure resistor use P<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub>²/R.

traps: D = T<sub>on</sub>/T, never T<sub>off</sub>/T. 0.4 ms on in a 1 ms period is D = 0.4, not 0.6.
V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub> is average. A true-RMS meter reads V<sub>s</sub>·√D, a different number.
Same on-time at double frequency doubles D; power rises four times because V<sub>o</sub> and I<sub>o</sub> both double.
The freewheeling diode holds load voltage near zero in off-time and carries inductive current. Without it the switch sees a large turn-off spike.
A chopper works on DC. AC voltage controllers and cycloconverters work on AC (see AC voltage controllers: phase and on-off control).

quiz.q: Define the duty ratio of a chopper and state its range.
quiz.a: D = T<sub>on</sub>/T = T<sub>on</sub>/(T<sub>on</sub> + T<sub>off</sub>), where T is switching period; 0 ≤ D ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Name the three control strategies used to set the duty ratio of a chopper.
Why is a freewheeling diode connected across an inductive load in a chopper?
quiz.a: Inductor current cannot change instantly. When the switch opens, the diode gives it a path, holds load voltage near zero, and protects the switch from a large turn-off voltage spike.

quiz.q: A chopper runs from a 150 V DC source at 5 kHz with an on-time of 0.12 ms. Find the period, the duty ratio and the average output voltage.
A 24 V source feeds an R-L load (R = 6 Ω, continuous current) through a chopper with D = 0.25. Find the average output voltage, current and power.
quiz.a: V<sub>o</sub> = 0.25 × 24 V = 6 V. I<sub>o</sub> = 6 V / 6 Ω = 1 A. P<sub>o</sub> = 6 V × 1 A = 6 W.

quiz.q: A chopper keeps its on-time fixed while the switching frequency is doubled. Which control strategy is this, and what happens to D, V<sub>o</sub> and P<sub>o</sub> for a continuous-current load?
quiz.a: Variable-frequency control. The period halves, so D doubles; V<sub>o</sub> doubles; I<sub>o</sub> doubles; P<sub>o</sub> goes up four times.

quiz.q: A designer claims variable-frequency control makes the output filter smaller. Evaluate that claim.
quiz.a: Partly wrong. The filter must smooth ripple at the lowest f<sub>s</sub> used, because the longest off-time gives the largest ripple. A low lowest frequency needs a larger filter. Variable-frequency control gives fixed pulse width and predictable peak current. Noise spreads over a band: lower peak at any one frequency, but harder filter and EMI clearance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Two- and four-quadrant choppers let a DC motor return braking energy to the source, as in traction and metro drives. Peak current-mode control, where an inner loop ends the pulse at a current threshold, is common in switching regulator ICs. Wide-band-gap switches such as SiC and GaN push chopper frequencies into hundreds of kHz and shrink the inductor (see Wide band-gap devices: SiC and GaN). Digital control with DSP or FPGA replaces the sawtooth comparator. Search: four-quadrant chopper, peak current-mode control, constant on-time control.
